newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FOCUS-Analysts welcome Taiwan's dual-listing reform.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Analysts welcome Taiwan's dual-listing reform.

text.p: Stock analysts on Wednesday hailed Taiwan's lifting of its ban on simultaneous local and offshore share listings, saying the liberalisation afforded new flexibility in capital formation for local and foreign firms.

"It surely is positive news that will help expand our capital market, helping local firms raise funds overseas and vice versa for foreign companies in Taiwan," said Allen Huang of National Securities.

The Securities and Futures Commission said on Tuesday that, effective immediately, it was lifting a restriction that prevented firms from listing shares simultaneously in Taiwan's stock exchange and foreign bourses.
Analysts said significant reaction on the trading floor was unlikely, but predicted the move would have long-term benefits for local and foreign firms in their fund-raising.
"The effect should be long-term, though I cannot yet see how big the impact will be," Huang said.
Huang was sceptical, however, as to whether the liberalisation would draw foreign listings to Taiwan's two exchanges.
"I'm not sure if the opening can attract foreign firms to list in Taiwan because they have to consider the local market's liquidity, volatility and price-earnings ratio levels," he said.

Watchdog commission officials said the liberalisation was expected also to open the door to speculation on price spreads between shares listed on multiple exchanges, increasing linkages between Taiwan and other markets.

Analysts said this, in turn, would draw more international attention to Taiwan's market, promoting stock trading across exchanges and better integrating Taiwan's firms and exchanges into the global financial system.
"By listing at foreign exchanges, Taiwan's firms will gain international awareness and can attract more foreign investors to invest," said Alex Chen of HSBC James Capel Taiwan Ltd.

Commission officials said the liberalisation applied to most major overseas exchanges, including the New York, Nasdaq and Amex in the United States and the main exchanges in London, Frankfurt, Tokyo, Osaka, Paris, Amsterdam, Singapore, Sydney, Kuala Lumpur and Bangkok.
Exchanges in arch rival communist China, including the Hong Kong stock exchange, are not included, officials said.
Until now, Taiwan firms listed in Taiwan have been barred from listing shares simultaneously on overseas exchanges.

Since 1992, overseas firms with shares listed in overseas markets have been allowed to tap into Taiwan's share market only through the issuance of Taiwan depository receipts. None has done so to date.

On the other hand, Taiwan firms have been active in listing shares on overseas markets, chiefly through global depository receipts or American depository receipts, as well as through primary listings by overseas-registered subsidiaries.
